Andrew Huberman on how Silicon Valley changed after Steve Jobs:

"What's unique about the Bay Area is that people care about the past, but it's really about what's happening now and the future.

There's not a lot of pomp and circumstance.

If you were to go to Cafe Borrone in Menlo Park in the early 2000s, you'd see somebody who had founded a huge company and is a billionaire, and they were just around. 

No one cared.

What's changed since Steve Jobs is that now the technologists are celebrities.

In the Bay Area, it used to be you wanted to do something that exported everywhere, but you were sort of invisible.

It was cool mostly because it was about the stuff people were doing and less about the people. And I sort of wish for that more."

Another of this market's ongoing divergences can be found in the oil markets. We have been recommending Brent oil longs and avoiding WTI to protect against the risks of SPR drains, export bans and domestic market manipulation ahead of midterms. Since August there is nearly a ~10% performance differential between the two.

At the time, Brent-WTI spreads were near the lows of the year. Now with them back to the highs, this view has less conviction behind it but I don't yet see a strong reason to change. The spread has seen much higher during historical geopolitical events and the US SPR has been drained significantly, meaning the idiosyncratic juice to squeeze out of WTI has materially decreased. If anything, there is probably risk of future export controls expanding to include crude also in order to refill the SPR which could increase the divergence further.

Recent developments from frontier Physical AI companies are showing that robots are capable of moving from single task automation to complete workflow automation.

This unlocks a market an order of magnitude larger than single task autonomy. Similar to the jump from L3 to L4 driving automation that allowed Waymo to start scaling its operations or the jump from AI chatbots to AI agents. 

Less than 5% of physical work in the world is actually single task. Machine tending, packaging, simple assembly. A lot of work, even if seemingly repetitive, require more higher level decision making than we think.

Take for example Dyna's recent demonstration for their laundry physical agent. Addressable annual laundry labor itself is ~$9.5B. 85% of North America's 59,000 hotels have 200 rooms or fewer. These have on average one full time laundry attendant. 

That laundry attendant is continuously navigating multiple decision trees - when to load the washer, when to transfer from washer to dryer, when to fold laundry, when to move folded stacks to the shelves, etc. Correctly making these decisions requires real scene understanding, memory, and the ability to reliably execute a large number of subtasks.

A laundry attendant that has a single task folding robot still needs to be near the laundry room for most of their shift since they need to support the robot in loading, unloading, transfering stacks and moving laundry baskets.

They free up some time, but they can't effectively reallocate it to housekeeping due to the constant support required. When a robot is able to complete entire laundry workflows unattended, now the hotel manager can quickly fill a real laundry attendent hiring need with a robot or reallocate an attendant to housekeeping work.  

The ability to complete entire workflows makes robots much more useful to businesses. This is the value of physical agents.

$ZIM: Own It, Don’t Trade It

The question investors keep asking is simple: when do you sell $ZIM? After all, we’ve had a run from $13 all the way to $30.

My answer: you probably don’t.

There are essentially two scenarios.

In the first, $ZIM gets acquired around the discussed $35 level. From roughly $30.50 today, that would mean about $4.50 of capital upside, with potentially another ~$5 in dividends. That puts the potential total return near 30%.

The second scenario is that the deal does not happen.

It is impossible to know how many investors currently own $ZIM mainly because of the takeover possibility. If the deal falls apart, disappointment and momentum alone could push the stock toward $27.

But that would not change the fundamental story.

By year-end, I expect $ZIM to have more than $30 per share in cash while the business remains profitable. A profitable company trading below the cash sitting on its balance sheet is not something I would panic about.

In fact, around $27 may prove to be close to a fundamental floor.

And if there is no acquisition, management will eventually have to decide what to do with all that cash.

The obvious answers are dividends, share buybacks, or both.

From my sources, significant buybacks have already been discussed with management by Israeli investors. If $ZIM remains independent, it could end up offering one of the highest dividend yields in the market, one of the largest buyback programs, or some combination of the two.

So the setup looks unusually simple.

If the buyout happens, shareholders get paid.

If it does not happen, the stock may initially fall, but investors are left owning a profitable company trading around or below its cash value, with enormous potential for capital returns.

That is why I see very little reason to sell $ZIM over the next two years.

Sometimes the best decision in investing is simply not touching the position.

There are essentially two scenarios.

In the first, $ZIM gets acquired around the discussed $35 level. From roughly $30.50 today, that would mean about $4.50 of capital upside, with potentially another ~$5 in dividends. That puts the potential total return near 30%.

The second scenario is that the deal does not happen.

It is impossible to know how many investors currently own $ZIM mainly because of the takeover possibility. If the deal falls apart, disappointment and momentum alone could push the stock toward $27.

But that would not change the fundamental story.

By year-end, I expect $ZIM to have more than $30 per share in cash while the business remains profitable. A profitable company trading below the cash sitting on its balance sheet is not something I would panic about.

In fact, around $27 may prove to be close to a fundamental floor.

And if there is no acquisition, management will eventually have to decide what to do with all that cash.

The obvious answers are dividends, share buybacks, or both.

From my sources, significant buybacks have already been discussed with management by Israeli investors. If $ZIM remains independent, it could end up offering one of the highest dividend yields in the market, one of the largest buyback programs, or some combination of the two.

So the setup looks unusually simple.

If the buyout happens, shareholders get paid.

If it does not happen, the stock may initially fall, but investors are left owning a profitable company trading around or below its cash value, with enormous potential for capital returns.

That is why I see very little reason to sell $ZIM over the next two years.

Sometimes the best decision in investing is simply not touching the position.

By my measurement, the efficiency of intelligence output is doubling roughly every five months. 

This isn't the models getting a bit better... this is the actual amount of intelligence you get out of each unit of energy, doubling, every five months... and the doubling time is shrinking.

Nothing in human history has compounded like this. Not electricity, not the internet. And there's no playbook for it, because every institution we have was built for a world where things changed over decades.

This is what I call The Economic Singularity. Somewhere around 2030 to 2032 the machine economy starts moving faster than the instruments we use to measure it... GDP, earnings, the wage were all built for a world of scarce human labour, all pointed at an economy that no longer runs on it. 

Which means the years between now and then are the window. The whole game is to be positioned on the scarce side of the ledger before the old numbers stop meaning anything, because once the machines are running the machine economy the easy part is over. 

We have maybe five years...
